The Six-Day War (1967) and Jerusalem
Israel's capture of East Jerusalem in June 1967 marks the end, or the beginning of the end, of the 'times of the Gentiles' (Luke 21:24).

Many popular dispensational writers; L. Nelson Bell, editor of Christianity Today, wrote in July 1967 that Jerusalem being completely in Jewish hands for the first time in more than two thousand years gave the Bible student a thrill and renewed faith in Scripture.

Jesus said Jerusalem would be 'trampled underfoot by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24), implying a time when that trampling would end. From AD 70 to 1967, apart from brief exceptions, Jerusalem was ruled by Gentile powers; in 1967 the whole city came under Jewish rule. Zechariah 12–14 sets the final conflict around Jerusalem, so a Jewish Jerusalem is a necessary precondition of the end-time scenario.

Luke 21:24 most naturally refers to Roman rule after AD 70, and the 'times of the Gentiles' may refer to the whole period of Gentile mission and dominance rather than to a political transfer. If 1967 ended the times of the Gentiles, the verse should mark the end of the age, yet Gentiles still control the Temple Mount (administered by the Islamic Waqf), so the 'fulfilment' is partial at best. Amillennial and preterist critics read the New Testament Jerusalem hope as fulfilled in the heavenly Jerusalem (Galatians 4:25–26; Hebrews 12:22). Historically, 1967 also produced a new generation count (1967 + 40 = 2007) that failed.

Many dispensationalists accept that the Temple Mount remains under Gentile control and therefore say the times of the Gentiles have not yet ended; they treat 1967 as significant stage-setting, not fulfilment. Some emphasise that the Gentile 'times' run until Christ's return (Daniel 2:44), so no modern event can complete them. Scholars such as Thomas Ice warn against tying 1967 to any timetable.

1967 was a dramatic event that many Christians, not only dispensationalists, found moving in the light of Luke 21:24. But the text's own wording, and the continuing Gentile authority over the Temple Mount, mean it cannot be confidently called a fulfilment; careful premillennial scholars themselves stop short of that, and generation counts from 1967 have already failed.
The 'terminal generation': 40, 70, 80 and 100-year counts
1970 to the present
The generation alive when Israel was reborn (or Jerusalem recaptured) will see Christ return; since a generation is 40, 70, 80 or 100 years, the end can be bracketed.
Hal Lindsey (1948 + about 40); Edgar Whisenant (1988); Chuck Smith (1981); later writers proposing 1948 + 70 (Psalm 90:10) = 2018, 1948 + 80 = 2028, or 100 years (Genesis 15:13–16).

Jesus said 'this generation will not pass away until all these things take place' (Matthew 24:34) immediately after the fig-tree parable. If the fig tree is Israel and its budding is 1948, the generation that saw it will see the end. Psalm 90:10 gives seventy or eighty years as a lifetime, so those born around 1948 would see the end within their lives.

Every count tied to 1948 or 1967 that reached its date has failed: 1981, 1988, 2007 and 2018 all passed. Exegetically, 'this generation' in Matthew consistently means Jesus' contemporaries (Matthew 11:16; 12:39–45; 23:36), which preterists and many other interpreters take to point to AD 70; even those who disagree recognise that the text gives no starting point in 1948. Jesus immediately adds that no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), a warning that sits uneasily with bracketing calculations. The method also changes the length of a generation whenever a date passes, which makes it unfalsifiable.

Mainstream dispensational scholars largely reject the terminal-generation calculation. Thomas Ice argues that 'this generation' is the generation that sees the signs of Matthew 24:4–31 during the future tribulation, so no count from 1948 is possible; others read genea as 'race' (Israel will not pass away). John Walvoord, though he saw Israel's return as highly significant, stressed that the rapture is signless and imminent and warned against dates. They regard Lindsey's and Whisenant's counts as errors of popular teaching, not of the system.

The terminal-generation idea is the most clearly falsified strand of modern prophecy teaching, and leading dispensational scholars have themselves abandoned it. The underlying question of what 'this generation' means remains a genuine exegetical debate (contemporaries and AD 70, the tribulation generation, or the Jewish race), but no reading supports counting forward from 1948.
The European Union as a revived Roman Empire and the ten kings
1957 to the present
The European Economic Community, now the European Union, is the revived fourth (Roman) empire of Daniel 2 and 7, from which ten kings and the Antichrist will arise.

Hal Lindsey (who in 1970 expected a ten-nation Common Market), many prophecy broadcasters, and in more cautious form scholars such as John Walvoord and Mark Hitchcock who expect a future revived Roman confederacy.

Daniel's fourth empire (Rome) ends with ten toes or ten horns (Daniel 2:41–44; 7:7, 24), and Revelation 13 and 17 describe ten kings who give power to the beast. Since Rome never existed in a ten-king form, there must be a future revival. The 1957 Treaty of Rome, and the integration of Europe from former Roman lands, look like the beginnings of such a revival, and the EEC reached ten members in 1981.

The EEC passed ten members in 1986 and the EU now has twenty-seven (after the United Kingdom left in 2020), so the ten-nation identification failed on its own terms; its territory also does not match the Roman Empire, which centred on the Mediterranean, including North Africa and the Middle East. Historicists read the ten horns as the kingdoms into which Rome broke after the fifth century; preterists apply Revelation 17's ten kings to client rulers of first-century Rome; amillennialists see recurring patterns of beastly power. Many critics also note that Daniel 2:44 places the coming of God's kingdom 'in the days of those kings', which the New Testament presents as beginning with Christ (Mark 1:15).

Dispensational scholars usually concede that the EEC/EU is not itself the ten-king confederacy and that the number of member states is irrelevant; they say the ten kings arise in the tribulation, possibly from regions rather than present nations, and that European integration is at most a trend consistent with prophecy. They maintain that the gap between Rome's fall and its revival is like other prophetic gaps (Daniel 9:26–27).

The specific identification of the Common Market or EU with the ten kings has been falsified and is now rarely pressed by scholars; the broader futurist expectation of a future Roman-type confederacy stands or falls with the futurist reading of Daniel 2 and 7, which remains a live but contested position.
Russia, Iran and Turkey as Gog and Magog (Ezekiel 38–39)
1917 to the present; revived after 2015

Ezekiel's invasion of Israel by 'Gog, of the land of Magog, the prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal', allied with Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer and Beth-togarmah, describes a future attack led by Russia with Iran, Turkey and others.

The Scofield Reference Bible (1909/1917), Hal Lindsey, John Walvoord, Mark Hitchcock, Joel Rosenberg and many others; Russia's military role in Syria from 2015 and its ties with Iran and Turkey renewed the claim.

The invader comes from 'the uttermost parts of the north' (Ezekiel 38:6, 15), and the land directly north of Israel at the greatest distance is Russia. Persia is modern Iran; Gomer and Beth-togarmah lay in modern Turkey. The invasion happens after Israel has been regathered 'from many peoples' and dwells securely (38:8), which had never happened before 1948. The coalition matches present alignments remarkably.

Most modern translations and Hebrew scholars read rosh as 'chief' ('the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal'), not as a place name, and the old link of Rosh with 'Russia', Meshech with 'Moscow' and Tubal with 'Tobolsk' rests on sound-alike etymology now rejected even by many futurists. Meshech and Tubal appear in Assyrian records as peoples of Anatolia (Mushki and Tabal), in modern Turkey, not Russia. Wilson's Armageddon Now! documents how the identification of 'the king of the north' shifted with the news for decades. Amillennialists note that Revelation 20:8 uses Gog and Magog for the nations of the whole world at the end, so the names became symbolic; Daniel Block reads Gog as an archetypal enemy; some preterists, such as Gary DeMar, place the fulfilment in the time of Esther. The battle's weapons (horses, bows, shields) also resist a literal modern reading.

Some dispensational scholars (for example Mark Hitchcock) still argue that Rosh is a proper name and point to Russia by geography; others concede that the Russia etymology is weak and identify the northern coalition by direction only. Most say the ancient names indicate the regions from which the invaders will come, whatever their present names. They answer the weapons objection by saying Ezekiel used the military terms his readers knew. Many caution that current alliances are not fulfilment and may change, as they have before.

That Ezekiel 38–39 describes a future end-time attack on Israel is a coherent futurist reading, though contested by amillennial, symbolic and preterist interpreters. The specific identification with Russia rests on weak etymology and on geography, and the history of shifting identifications counsels great caution; the strongest futurist presentations now treat present alliances as illustrations rather than evidence.
Wars and rumours of wars in the Middle East
Repeated wars involving Israel and its neighbours, the Gulf Wars and recent conflicts with Gaza and Iran show that the end-time conflict around Jerusalem is approaching.

Prophecy broadcasters and popular writers from the 1967 and 1973 wars onward; John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis (1974, revised 1990, later updated); many voices again after the Hamas attack on Israel of 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza, and after the Iranian missile strikes on Israel in 2024 and the June 2025 exchange of strikes between Israel and Iran, in which the United States also struck Iranian nuclear sites.

Scripture places the final battles around Israel and Jerusalem (Zechariah 12 and 14; Joel 3; Revelation 16:16). Only since 1948 has a Jewish state existed for nations to attack, and the region has become the focus of global attention and conflict, as Zechariah 12:3 ('a cup of staggering to all the surrounding peoples') suggests. Jesus listed 'wars and rumours of wars' among the signs (Matthew 24:6–7).

Jesus' words cut the other way: 'see that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet' (Matthew 24:6). Wars are the ordinary condition of history, not proof of the end, and the Middle East has seen wars in every century. Every major conflict since 1948 (1956, 1967, 1973, 1982, 1991, 2003, 2006, 2014, 2023–24, 2025) has been announced by someone as the prelude to Armageddon, and none was. Preterists read Zechariah 14 and the Olivet signs in relation to AD 70 and Christ's first-century work; amillennialists see the 'last days' as the whole church age. Critics also warn that reading the news as prophecy can harden political positions and make it harder to see the human suffering on all sides.

Careful dispensational writers agree that Matthew 24:6 forbids alarm and that ordinary wars are not signs of the end; they say that these conflicts are consistent with the biblical picture and remind believers that God's purposes include Israel, but that the specific battles of Ezekiel 38 and Armageddon are still future and unidentifiable before the rapture. Many explicitly warn against declaring any present war to be Gog or Armageddon.

That the Middle East is a recurring centre of conflict is undeniable, and futurists see this as consistent with Zechariah's picture. But Jesus himself said wars do not mean the end is here, and the track record of announcing each conflict as the final one is uniformly negative. Christians of all views can agree to pray for peace and for all who suffer in the region, without treating any party's actions as a prophetic timetable.
Rebuilding Babylon in Iraq
1980s to 2003; still argued
The literal city of Babylon on the Euphrates must be rebuilt to be destroyed as Revelation 17–18 and Jeremiah 50–51 describe; Saddam Hussein's reconstruction was the beginning.
Charles Dyer (The Rise of Babylon, 1991), Andy Woods and other dispensational writers; Henry Morris and some earlier futurists.

Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50–51 describe a sudden, total destruction of Babylon, never to be inhabited again, which historically did not happen: Cyrus took Babylon without destroying it, and it declined slowly over centuries. Since prophecy must be fulfilled exactly, a future Babylon must rise and fall. Revelation 18's commercial details fit a literal city, and oil wealth made such a rise plausible.

Most interpreters read 'Babylon' in Revelation as a symbolic name, as 1 Peter 5:13 uses it for Rome: Revelation 17:9 places the woman on 'seven hills', and 17:18 calls her 'the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth', which in John's day was Rome. Preterists such as Kenneth Gentry identify Babylon as apostate Jerusalem. Prophetic language of total desolation is often hyperbolic or conditional (Jeremiah 18:7–10), and Babylon did become desolate in the long run. Saddam's project ended with his fall; Babylon is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and an archaeological park, not a rising world capital.

Dyer and Woods maintain that the case for a future literal Babylon does not depend on Saddam and that the Old Testament prophecies remain unfulfilled; Dyer issued an updated edition in 2003 and has continued to argue for a future Babylon independently of Saddam's project. Other dispensationalists, however, accept that Revelation's Babylon may be symbolic of a world system or a different city, showing that the literal-Babylon view is not a test of dispensational orthodoxy.

The future-Babylon thesis is a minority position even among futurists, and its moment of greatest plausibility (Saddam's rebuilding) has passed. It raises a real question about how fully Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50–51 were fulfilled, but the symbolic reading of Revelation's Babylon has strong textual support and is held across preterist, idealist, historicist and many futurist interpreters.
The Third Temple movement and red heifers
1967 to the present

Preparations by Jewish groups to rebuild the Temple, including the making of vessels and the search for an unblemished red heifer for purification (Numbers 19), show that the Temple of the tribulation is near.

Thomas Ice and Randall Price (Ready to Rebuild, 1992), Grant Jeffrey, many prophecy broadcasters; some Christians have helped Jewish groups raise red heifers. Jewish groups such as the Temple Institute (founded 1987) pursue rebuilding for their own religious reasons.

Daniel 9:27, Matthew 24:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and Revelation 11:1–2 speak of an end-time temple in which sacrifices cease and the man of lawlessness takes his seat. A temple therefore must be built. The detailed preparations, from priestly garments to the 2022 arrival of red heifers from Texas, show the plan is not imaginary.

Many interpreters read these passages as fulfilled in AD 70 (Matthew 24:15 with Luke 21:20) or as referring to the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 2:21), and Hebrews teaches that Christ's sacrifice ended the need for animal sacrifice (Hebrews 8:13; 10:11–18), so critics see no positive theological reason to expect, still less to encourage, a rebuilt temple. Red heifer announcements have come and gone since at least 1997, when a calf named Melody was declared a candidate and later disqualified. Critics such as Gershom Gorenberg warn that Christian support for Temple activism on the Temple Mount, one of the most sensitive sites in the world, risks contributing to violence.

Ice and Price argue that their view is about what Scripture predicts, not what Christians should cause, and that a future temple, even if it is built in unbelief, is the setting the passages require; they deny that a rebuilt temple implies any return to sacrifice for Christians. Most dispensational scholars say they neither fund nor encourage Temple Mount activism and stress that the rapture is imminent regardless of whether preparations advance.

The expectation of a future temple follows from a futurist reading of Daniel 9, 2 Thessalonians 2 and Revelation 11 and is a coherent position, but it is contested by strong preterist and typological readings. Present-day preparations are real but depend on Jewish religious and Israeli political decisions; treating each red heifer as a prophetic milestone has repeatedly proved premature, and the ethical concerns about encouraging Temple Mount activism deserve to be taken seriously by all sides.
The US embassy move to Jerusalem (2018)
December 2017 to May 2018
US recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital (6 December 2017) and the opening of the embassy there on 14 May 2018, seventy years after Israel's independence, was a prophetic milestone.
Some prophecy broadcasters and social-media commentators; evangelical pastors John Hagee and Robert Jeffress took part in the opening ceremony, chiefly as supporters of Israel.

God promised to bless those who bless Abraham's descendants (Genesis 12:3), and Zechariah 12 places Jerusalem at the centre of the nations' attention in the last days. International recognition of a Jewish capital in Jerusalem, timed to the seventieth anniversary of 1948 (recalling Jeremiah's seventy years), seemed to many a significant moment in God's purposes.

No biblical text mentions foreign embassies or recognition by Gentile powers. The 'seventy years' link is numerological coincidence based on the Gregorian calendar. Critics, including many evangelicals, worried that framing a contested political decision as prophecy fuses theology with partisan politics and ignores Palestinian Christians and the complex questions of justice and peace in the land. Preterist and amillennial critics deny that the modern city of Jerusalem has the prophetic role claimed for it.

Most dispensational scholars presented the move as a welcome act of support for Israel consistent with Genesis 12:3, not as the fulfilment of any specific prophecy, and said so explicitly. They argued that political support for Israel is a separate question from eschatology, even if many supporters hold both convictions.

The embassy move is best understood as a political event that many Christian Zionists welcomed, not as a predicted prophetic event; few serious premillennial scholars claimed otherwise. Christians of different views continue to debate the theology of the land and its implications for justice, peace and Palestinian Christians, a debate that deserves to be conducted on its own terms rather than through prophecy timetables.
Global government, the United Nations and globalisation
1920 to the present
The League of Nations, the United Nations, the World Economic Forum and globalisation are steps towards the one-world government of the beast.
Many twentieth-century prophecy writers (some saw the League of Nations as the beast's forerunner); Tim LaHaye's and Jerry Jenkins' Left Behind novels; numerous broadcasters.

Revelation 13:7–8 gives the beast authority 'over every tribe and people and language and nation', and 17:12–13 has the kings hand power to him. Before modern communications and international institutions such rule was unimaginable; today global institutions, trade, communications and surveillance make it technically conceivable for the first time.

Biblical 'whole world' language often means the known world of the time (Luke 2:1; Acts 11:28; Colossians 1:6), and the first readers would have heard Revelation 13 as a portrait of Rome's claim to universal rule, which preterists and idealists see as its primary reference. Historically, the identification has jumped from the League of Nations to the UN, the EEC, the 'New World Order' after 1991 and later bodies; none has gained anything like world sovereignty, and nationalism has resurged in many places. Critics also warn that suspicion of all international cooperation can feed conspiracy theories and distract from the church's call to seek the good of the city (Jeremiah 29:7).

Dispensational scholars generally say that the beast's government will arise only after the rapture and that present institutions are at most precursors or 'trends'; some deny the UN has any prophetic role. Many stress that Christians should obey legitimate authorities (Romans 13) while being alert to idolatrous claims by any state.

That powers may make totalitarian and idolatrous claims is a permanent biblical warning, applicable to Rome and every later empire; whether Revelation 13 also predicts a single future world government is debated between futurists and other schools. The specific identifications of modern institutions have shifted constantly and should be held very loosely.
Cashless payments, RFID chips and the mark of the beast
1970s to the present
Universal product codes, credit cards, social security numbers, implanted RFID microchips, digital currencies and biometric payments are the technology of the mark of the beast.
Mary Stewart Relfe (When Your Money Fails, 1981) and many later popular writers; the theme features prominently in prophecy media and fiction.

Revelation 13:16–17 says no one can buy or sell without the mark on the right hand or forehead. Only in the modern age has technology made it possible to monitor and control every economic transaction; implanted chips (such as the VeriChip, approved in the United States in 2004) and cashless societies match the text remarkably closely.

The text makes the mark a sign of worship and allegiance to the beast (Revelation 13:15–16; 14:9–11), parallel to the seal of God on the foreheads of his servants (7:3; 14:1), which no one thinks is a literal tattoo; the imagery likely echoes Deuteronomy 6:8 and the stamp (charagma) of imperial authority on coins and documents. Preterist and idealist critics note that first-century Christians in Asia faced economic exclusion for refusing emperor worship and trade-guild idolatry (Revelation 2:14, 20). The identification has moved from barcodes to credit cards, chips, vaccines and digital currencies, and the original candidates are now ordinary. Fear of accidentally taking the mark contradicts the text's picture of a deliberate choice.

Many dispensational scholars agree that the mark is an act of worship and loyalty that cannot be taken by accident, and that present technologies are not the mark; they argue only that such technologies show how the economic control of Revelation 13 could be implemented, and that the mark itself will be imposed after the rapture. Some believe the mark will be literal and visible, as well as signifying allegiance.

Almost all interpreters now agree that the mark of the beast is fundamentally about worship and allegiance, not a technology one could take unawares. Futurists may reasonably note that modern technology makes total economic control feasible, but the chain of specific identifications has proved unreliable, and pastoral harm (fear, refusal of ordinary services) is a real cost.
Earthquakes, famines and pandemics increasing
Ongoing
Earthquakes, famines and plagues are increasing in frequency and intensity, like birth pains, showing the end is near.
Many popular prophecy teachers and websites, often citing larger numbers of reported earthquakes; COVID-19 revived the claim.

Jesus listed famines, earthquakes in various places and pestilences as 'the beginning of birth pains' (Matthew 24:7–8; Luke 21:11). Birth pains grow more frequent and intense as delivery approaches, so increasing disasters indicate approaching birth of the new age. Modern disasters affect larger populations and are seen worldwide instantly.

The data do not support an increase in the relevant sense. The US Geological Survey explains that the number of large earthquakes (magnitude 7 and above) has stayed fairly constant over the instrumental record; more earthquakes are recorded because there are far more seismographs. Famine deaths have fallen dramatically since the mid-twentieth century relative to earlier decades and to population, according to Our World in Data. COVID-19 was a grave pandemic (WHO counted around seven million confirmed deaths, with estimates of excess deaths considerably higher), but it was smaller relative to population than the 1918 influenza or the Black Death, which earlier Christians also took as signs. Exegetically, Jesus said these things are 'the beginning of birth pains' and 'the end is not yet' (Matthew 24:6, 8), and the 'birth pains' image signals inevitability and suffering more than a measurable acceleration curve.

Careful premillennialists accept that the 'increase' claim is often statistically unsound and that these signs characterise the whole age; some argue that 'birth pains' implies intensification only in the tribulation itself, when the seal judgments of Revelation 6 bring famine and death on an unprecedented scale. They prefer to say that disasters remind believers of the fallenness of creation (Romans 8:22) and of the need for readiness, not that they date the end.

On the empirical claim the critics are right: major earthquakes are not measurably increasing, famine mortality has fallen, and pandemics are not new. The theological point that disasters are 'birth pains' of a groaning creation awaiting redemption is shared across all views; what fails is the attempt to turn them into a measurable countdown.
Knowledge increasing and travel (Daniel 12:4)
'Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased' (Daniel 12:4) predicts the explosion of travel, science and information technology in the modern age.

Popular prophecy writers since the nineteenth century; a story circulates that Isaac Newton predicted travel at fifty miles an hour from this verse and was mocked by Voltaire, but the anecdote is poorly attested.

Daniel was told to seal the book 'until the time of the end', when many would run to and fro and knowledge would increase. For millennia travel and knowledge advanced slowly; in the last two centuries they have exploded. This unique development fits the verse and its 'time of the end' setting.

In context, the 'knowledge' is understanding of Daniel's sealed prophecy, and 'running to and fro' (compare Amos 8:12, where people 'run to and fro to seek the word of the Lord') describes searching for that understanding. Many modern translations reflect this. Daniel 12:4 is therefore about understanding the prophecy as it is fulfilled, not about technology, and early Christians already saw it in the light of Christ's revelation (1 Peter 1:10–12). Every age of rapid change (the printing press, steam, the telegraph) has been fitted to the verse.

Some dispensational scholars accept that the primary meaning concerns understanding of prophecy, but suggest that the increase of prophetic understanding in the end time could coincide with general increase of knowledge; others continue to read it more broadly. Most would not build an argument for the nearness of the end on this verse alone.

The technological reading is popular but exegetically weak, and the contextual reading (increasing understanding of Daniel's prophecy) is widely held, including by many futurists. The verse is better used to encourage humble study than as a sign of the times.
Artificial intelligence and the image of the beast
2010s to the present

The image of the beast that is given 'breath' so that it can speak and cause those who refuse to worship it to be killed (Revelation 13:14–15) describes artificial intelligence, robots, holograms or deepfake media.
Popular prophecy commentators, YouTube teachers and some authors, especially since the spread of large language models in the 2020s.

For centuries a speaking image seemed impossible except by demonic power; now machines can generate speech, images and apparently intelligent responses. An AI system controlling surveillance and economic access could enforce the worship and the mark described in Revelation 13. This is the first generation in which the passage can be read literally without resorting to the supernatural.

First readers would have recognised the image against the background of emperor statues and the imperial cult in Asia, and ancient religious showmen were known to make statues appear to speak (Lucian describes a fraudulent talking-snake oracle); the false prophet's 'great signs' (13:13) are deceptive wonders, not engineering. Earlier generations fitted the passage to television, computers and holograms. Interpreting every new technology as the image can breed fear of legitimate tools and distracts from the text's real point: the false worship of political power.

Dispensational scholars generally say the image is a future idol connected with the Antichrist in the tribulation, whose 'breath' may be supernatural deception; technology may help explain how it could work but should not be identified with it. Many caution against sensationalism about AI while sharing concerns about surveillance and idolatry of technology.

Ethical concerns about AI, surveillance and the idolising of human power are legitimate and are shared by Christians of every view. Identifying AI as the image of the beast is speculative, follows the long pattern of fitting each new technology to Revelation 13, and is not required by any futurist reading.
The apostasy of the church
The decline of churchgoing in the West, doctrinal liberalism and moral compromise are the great 'falling away' (2 Thessalonians 2:3) and the 'perilous times' of the last days (2 Timothy 3:1–5).
